初學者可先將長桿握持，使共鳴囊置於桿與弦之間；拉奏時以有缺口短棒或馬尾弓沿弦來回: A beginner can first hold the long stick so that the resonating bladder sits between the stick and the string; to bow, draw a notched short stick or a horsehair bow back and forth along the string. Stopping the string changes the pitch, while the open string is good for practising a simple accompaniment of one to three notes. In the struck type, turn the drum face to the side, hit it with the stick or a drumstick, then stamp the lower end on the ground so that the bells, cymbals or tambourine sound as they bounce; if it has a tuned string you can still draw a coarse tone from it. The beginner's task is to control the bowing pressure and the rhythm of the stamping foot.

拉弦版以粗腸線經豬膀胱共鳴，弓拉時產生持續或節奏性的嗡鳴音；音域有限，開放弦僅有: In the bowed version a thick gut string resonates through a pig's bladder, and bowing produces a continuous or rhythmic buzzing tone; the range is limited, an open string giving only one to three notes, and stopping the string changes the pitch. Bowing with a notched wooden stick gives a coarser tone. The struck version turns the drum face to the side, or sets bells, cymbals, wooden fish and other fittings sounding by hitting, stamping and bouncing; it can imitate a drum roll and impacts, and the volume rises with the force used. Compared with a plain bowed string instrument, its character lies in the combination of a resonating body and percussion fittings rather than in a steady melodic range.
早期琴身以長木桿構成，張一條或多條粗腸線，以豬膀胱作共鳴器；拉奏可用有缺口木棒或: The early body was a long wooden stick carrying one or more thick gut strings, with a pig's bladder as resonator; it could be bowed with a notched wooden stick or a horsehair bow. A Dutch variant replaces the bladder with a drum-shaped ring clamped between the stick and a single gut string. The modern struck type usually fits bells, wooden blocks, cymbals and a tambourine to the stick, with a spring and rubber at the bottom; some replace the gut string with a long spring, and some have no string at all. During the First World War tin cans and wooden boxes were also used as resonators.

By 1675 the Dutch had a bumbass, in which a drum-shaped ring replaced the pig's bladder, and it travelled with emigrants to the German-speaking communities of Pennsylvania and became the boomba, sounded by striking and stamping. The bladder fiddle is a folk instrument of Europe and the Americas, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321-7. In its original form it is a string instrument made of a long stick, one or more thick gut strings and a pig's bladder as resonator, bowed with a notched wooden stick or a horsehair bow. Until the early nineteenth century it was mostly played by travelling musicians and beggars, and it could also serve serious folk music or comic effect. It later split into two kinds: in Lithuania and elsewhere the bowed form survived, sounding a continuous or rhythmic bass; the other became a percussion instrument, struck and stamped in the folk music of Europe, North America and Australia, imitating drum sounds and other percussion colours.
膀胱提琴的聆聽場合主要見於民間音樂：歷史上由流浪樂手與乞丐演奏，可用於嚴肅民樂，: You mostly hear the bladder fiddle in folk music: historically it was played by travelling musicians and beggars, and it can serve serious folk music or work as humour. The traditional bowed version survives in Lithuania as a folk instrument and may be found in Estonia and Flanders, producing a continuous or rhythmic low drone; multi-string versions let the player accompany other instruments with simple figures. The struck version is used in the folk music of Europe, North America and Australia and can imitate a drum roll and other percussion effects; in the German-speaking culture of Pennsylvania it is played as a percussion instrument, and it appears at events in Texas that celebrate German heritage.
